text: What does a serum sodium result describe?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Sterns RH. Disorders of plasma sodium — causes, consequences, and correction. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(1):55–65.

Edelman IS, et al. Interrelations between serum sodium concentration, serum osmolarity and total exchangeable sodium, total exchangeable potassium and total body water. J Clin Invest. 1958;37(9):1236–56.

options.text: The total amount of sodium in the body
options.explanation: No. The lab cannot measure total body sodium from a blood sample.

options.text: The ratio of sodium to water in plasma
options.explanation: Correct. It is a concentration: sodium per litre, so it moves when either sodium or water changes.

options.text: The amount of sodium inside cells
options.explanation: No. Sodium is mostly outside cells; the result reflects plasma.

options.text: The sodium excreted in the urine each day
options.explanation: No. That needs a urine collection, not a serum sample.

explanation: Serum sodium is a concentration. It follows the ratio of exchangeable sodium (plus potassium) to total body water, so a low result usually means too much water rather than too little sodium.

text: Where is most of the body's potassium found?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Sterns RH. Disorders of plasma sodium — causes, consequences, and correction. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(1):55–65.
Cordeiro BM, Fontes CFL, Meyer-Fernandes JR. Molecular basis of Na, K–ATPase regulation of diseases. Int J Mol Sci. 2024;25(24):13398.

options.text: In plasma
options.explanation: No. Plasma potassium is only about 3.5–5 mmol/L, a small share of the total.

options.text: In the interstitial fluid
options.explanation: No. The interstitial fluid, like plasma, is part of the potassium-poor ECF.

options.text: Inside cells
options.explanation: Correct. The sodium pump keeps potassium inside cells and sodium outside.

options.text: In bone
options.explanation: No. Bone holds a store of sodium, not most of the potassium.

explanation: Sodium is mostly outside cells and potassium mostly inside. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in every cell membrane maintains that split.

text: What does the sodium pump (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) do?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Cordeiro BM, Fontes CFL, Meyer-Fernandes JR. Molecular basis of Na, K–ATPase regulation of diseases. Int J Mol Sci. 2024;25(24):13398.

options.text: Uses energy to move three sodium ions out of the cell for every two potassium ions in
options.explanation: Correct. This 3:2 exchange keeps sodium outside cells and potassium inside.

options.text: Uses energy to move two sodium ions out for every three potassium ions in
options.explanation: No. The ratio is the other way round: three sodium out, two potassium in.

options.text: Lets water cross the membrane
options.explanation: No. Water crosses through aquaporins and the lipid membrane, not the sodium pump.

options.text: Lets sodium flow into cells without using energy
options.explanation: No. The pump works against the gradient and uses ATP.

explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase hydrolyses ATP to export three sodium ions and import two potassium ions per cycle.

text: Where is ADH (vasopressin) made?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Tasker JG, et al. Advances in the neurophysiology of magnocellular neuroendocrine cells. J Neuroendocrinol. 2020;32(4):e12826.

options.text: In the posterior pituitary
options.explanation: No. The posterior pituitary stores and releases ADH but doesn't make it.

options.text: In nerve cells of the hypothalamus, which carry it to the posterior pituitary
options.explanation: Correct. It is made in the hypothalamus, carried down nerve fibres and released from the posterior pituitary.

options.text: In the adrenal cortex
options.explanation: No. The adrenal cortex makes aldosterone.

options.text: In the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney
options.explanation: No. Those cells release renin.

explanation: ADH is synthesised by magnocellular neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus, transported down their axons and released from the posterior pituitary.

text: A patient's plasma becomes more dilute over a few hours. What happens to their brain cells?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Sterns RH. Disorders of plasma sodium — causes, consequences, and correction. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(1):55–65.

options.text: They shrink
options.explanation: No. Cells shrink when plasma becomes more concentrated.

options.text: They swell
options.explanation: Correct. Water moves into the cells, towards the side with more dissolved particles.

options.text: Nothing, because sodium can't enter cells
options.explanation: No. It's water that moves, and water crosses cell membranes freely.

options.text: Nothing, because the sodium pump compensates
options.explanation: No. The pump keeps the ions apart; it doesn't stop water moving.

explanation: Water crosses cell membranes freely and moves until the concentration of dissolved particles is equal on both sides. Dilute plasma means water moves into cells, so they swell, which is why sodium disorders cause neurological symptoms.

text: Which hormone mainly controls how much water the kidney keeps?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Nielsen S, et al. Aquaporins in the kidney: from molecules to medicine. Physiol Rev. 2002;82(1):205–44.
Tsilosani A, Gao C, Zhang W. Aldosterone-regulated sodium transport and blood pressure. Front Physiol. 2022;13:770375.

options.text: Aldosterone
options.explanation: No. Aldosterone acts mainly on sodium reabsorption.

options.text: Atrial natriuretic peptide
options.explanation: No. ANP mainly increases sodium excretion.

options.text: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
options.explanation: Correct. ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct.

options.text: Angiotensin II
options.explanation: No. Angiotensin II drives aldosterone release and stimulates thirst and ADH, but doesn't itself open water channels.

explanation: ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells and moves aquaporin-2 into the urine-facing membrane, so water can be drawn back towards the salty medulla.

text: A 60 kg woman has a sodium of 138 mmol/L and about 30 L of total body water. She retains 1.5 L of water and loses no sodium. Estimate her new sodium.
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Sterns RH. Disorders of plasma sodium — causes, consequences, and correction. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(1):55–65.

Edelman IS, et al. Interrelations between serum sodium concentration, serum osmolarity and total exchangeable sodium, total exchangeable potassium and total body water. J Clin Invest. 1958;37(9):1236–56.

options.text: 125 mmol/L
options.explanation: No. That would need about 3 L of retained water.

options.text: 131 mmol/L
options.explanation: Correct. 138 × 30 / 31.5 ≈ 131 mmol/L.

options.text: 134 mmol/L
options.explanation: No. Check the arithmetic: the water rises by 5%, so the sodium falls by about 5%.

options.text: 138 mmol/L
options.explanation: No. The amount of sodium is unchanged, but it is now dissolved in more water.

explanation: Sodium concentration follows the ratio of sodium to water. With no change in body sodium: 138 × 30 / (30 + 1.5) ≈ 131 mmol/L. This simple form is an estimate.

text: A renin sample arrives in the lab sitting in ice water. What is the main risk?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Rutledge AC, et al. Survey of renin and aldosterone testing practices by Ontario laboratories. Pract Lab Med. 2021;25:e00229.

options.text: A falsely low renin from degradation
options.explanation: No. The main problem with cold is the opposite.

options.text: A falsely high renin from cryoactivation of prorenin
options.explanation: Correct. Cold converts inactive prorenin to active renin in the tube.

options.text: Haemolysis releasing renin from red cells
options.explanation: No. Red cells don't contain renin.

options.text: No effect, because chilling is recommended
options.explanation: No. Renin samples should stay at room temperature until separated and frozen.

explanation: Chilling a renin sample causes cryoactivation: prorenin becomes active renin and the result is falsely high. Keep renin samples at room temperature until the plasma is separated and frozen.

text: Plasma osmolality 270 mmol/kg, urine osmolality 410 mmol/kg, urine sodium 12 mmol/L, no diuretic given. What do the results suggest?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Schrier RW. Body fluid volume regulation in health and disease: a unifying hypothesis. Ann Intern Med. 1990;113(2):155–9.
Spasovski G, et al. Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia. Eur J Endocrinol. 2014;170(3):G1–47.

options.text: Primary polydipsia: ADH is switched off
options.explanation: No. With ADH off, urine would be maximally dilute, not 410 mmol/kg.

options.text: Low effective arterial blood volume: non-osmotic ADH is on and the kidney is keeping sodium
options.explanation: Correct. ADH is on despite dilute plasma, and the low urine sodium shows the RAAS holding sodium.

options.text: Diuretic effect
options.explanation: No. Diuretics usually raise urine sodium, and none was given.

options.text: A lab artefact: the plasma isn't really dilute
options.explanation: No. A measured osmolality of 270 mmol/kg confirms true hypotonicity.

explanation: Concentrated urine in dilute plasma means ADH is being driven by something other than osmolality. A urine sodium of 30 mmol/L or less with no diuretic points to low effective arterial blood volume, as in heart failure, cirrhosis or volume depletion.

text: A man with heart failure has oedema to both knees and a sodium of 125 mmol/L. Which explanation fits best?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Schrier RW. Body fluid volume regulation in health and disease: a unifying hypothesis. Ann Intern Med. 1990;113(2):155–9.
Filippatos TD, Elisaf MS. Hyponatremia in patients with heart failure. World J Cardiol. 2013;5(9):317–28.
Schrier RW, Abraham WT. Hormones and hemodynamics in heart failure. N Engl J Med. 1999;341(8):577–85.

options.text: He has lost sodium in his urine and needs sodium replacement
options.explanation: No. His body holds extra sodium; giving more adds to the oedema.

options.text: His arteries are underfilled, so the RAAS and non-osmotic ADH make the kidney keep sodium and even more water
options.explanation: Correct. He has extra sodium and even more extra water.

options.text: The low result is an artefact of oedema fluid in the sample
options.explanation: No. Oedema fluid isn't in a blood sample.

options.text: Aldosterone has made him lose water
options.explanation: No. Aldosterone makes the kidney keep sodium, not lose water.

explanation: In heart failure the weak pump leaves the arteries underfilled. Both systems respond as if the patient were dehydrated: the kidney keeps sodium (oedema) and non-osmotic ADH keeps even more water, so the sodium-to-water ratio falls.

text: What mainly sets the volume of the extracellular fluid?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Sterns RH. Disorders of plasma sodium — causes, consequences, and correction. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(1):55–65.

options.text: The amount of sodium in the body
options.explanation: Correct. Sodium is held outside cells, and water follows it to keep osmolality equal.

options.text: The amount of potassium in the body
options.explanation: No. Potassium is mainly inside cells.

options.text: The ADH level alone
options.explanation: No. ADH sets the concentration; volume follows the amount of sodium.

options.text: The plasma protein level alone
options.explanation: No. Proteins matter for fluid distribution across capillaries, but sodium sets ECF volume.

explanation: Sodium content sets the volume of the ECF; water balance sets the concentration. That's why the sodium system (RAAS, natriuretic peptides) regulates volume.

text: When ADH acts on the collecting duct, where are aquaporin-2 channels inserted?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Nielsen S, et al. Aquaporins in the kidney: from molecules to medicine. Physiol Rev. 2002;82(1):205–44.

options.text: Into the urine-facing (apical) membrane of the principal cells
options.explanation: Correct. That lets water enter the cell from the urine.

options.text: Into the blood-facing membrane of the principal cells
options.explanation: No. That side already has aquaporin-3 and -4.

options.text: Into the loop of Henle
options.explanation: No. ADH-regulated aquaporin-2 is in the collecting duct.

options.text: Into red cell membranes
options.explanation: No. Aquaporin-2 is a kidney collecting duct channel.

explanation: ADH binds V2 receptors on principal cells and moves aquaporin-2 from vesicles into the apical membrane. Water then leaves through aquaporin-3 and -4 on the blood side.

text: Why do labs measure copeptin instead of ADH?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Morgenthaler NG, et al. Assay for the measurement of copeptin, a stable peptide derived from the precursor of vasopressin. Clin Chem. 2006;52(1):112–9.

options.text: Copeptin is a stable fragment from the same precursor as ADH, so it stands in for ADH
options.explanation: Correct. ADH itself is unstable and hard to measure.

options.text: Copeptin is the active form of ADH
options.explanation: No. Copeptin has no known antidiuretic action.

options.text: Copeptin is made by the kidney in response to ADH
options.explanation: No. It comes from the same precursor molecule in the hypothalamus.

options.text: Copeptin measures aldosterone activity
options.explanation: No. It reflects ADH release.

explanation: Copeptin is cut from the same precursor as ADH and released in equal amounts. It is stable after collection, so it is used as a surrogate for ADH.

text: Which receptor does ADH bind to make the kidney keep water?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Nielsen S, et al. Aquaporins in the kidney: from molecules to medicine. Physiol Rev. 2002;82(1):205–44.

options.text: V1a receptor
options.explanation: No. V1a receptors mediate vasoconstriction.

options.text: V2 receptor
options.explanation: Correct. V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells trigger aquaporin-2 insertion.

options.text: Angiotensin II type 1 receptor
options.explanation: No. That is angiotensin II's receptor.

options.text: Mineralocorticoid receptor
options.explanation: No. That is aldosterone's receptor.

explanation: ADH acts on V2 receptors on the blood side of collecting duct principal cells; the signal (cyclic AMP) moves aquaporin-2 into the urine-facing membrane.

text: Why can the most concentrated urine reach only about 1,200 mmol/kg?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Sands JM, Layton HE. The physiology of urinary concentration: an update. Semin Nephrol. 2009;29(3):178–95.

options.text: Because aquaporin-2 can only open to a set size
options.explanation: No. The channels let water move; something else sets the limit.

options.text: Because urine can't become more concentrated than the inner medulla around the collecting duct
options.explanation: Correct. Water leaves the urine only while the surrounding tissue is saltier.

options.text: Because ADH levels have a fixed maximum
options.explanation: No. ADH opens the channels but doesn't set the ceiling.

options.text: Because the bladder reabsorbs water
options.explanation: No. The bladder doesn't concentrate urine.

explanation: The loops of Henle build an increasingly concentrated medulla, up to about 1,200 mmol/kg at the tip. With ADH acting, water leaves the collecting duct until the urine matches that tissue.

text: In human studies, at roughly what plasma osmolality does ADH switch on?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Hughes F, Mythen M, Montgomery H. The sensitivity of the human thirst response to changes in plasma osmolality: a systematic review. Perioper Med (Lond). 2018;7:1.
Sterns RH. Disorders of plasma sodium — causes, consequences, and correction. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(1):55–65.

options.text: About 270 mmol/kg
options.explanation: No. At 270 mmol/kg plasma is dilute and ADH should be off.

options.text: About 284 mmol/kg
options.explanation: Correct. Thirst starts at a similar point.

options.text: About 295 mmol/kg
options.explanation: No. That is near the top of the reference interval.

options.text: About 310 mmol/kg
options.explanation: No. That is well above the switch-on point.

explanation: ADH switches on at about 284 mmol/kg and the system responds to changes of only 1–2%. In sodium terms, ADH becomes detectable once sodium rises above about 135 mmol/L.

text: After a very salty meal, which system responds first?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Bichet DG. Regulation of thirst and vasopressin release. Annu Rev Physiol. 2019;81:359–73.

options.text: The water system: ADH and thirst
options.explanation: Correct. Osmolality rises first, so ADH and thirst respond.

options.text: The RAAS, which switches on
options.explanation: No. The RAAS is switched down as the ECF expands.

options.text: The natriuretic peptides, before anything else
options.explanation: No. They respond to volume stretching the heart, later in the sequence.

options.text: Neither: sodium is excreted unchanged
options.explanation: No. The extra sodium first raises osmolality.

explanation: Extra sodium raises osmolality, so osmoreceptors switch on ADH and thirst. As the ECF expands, the RAAS is switched down and the extra sodium is excreted.

text: How does aldosterone make the kidney keep sodium?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Tsilosani A, Gao C, Zhang W. Aldosterone-regulated sodium transport and blood pressure. Front Physiol. 2022;13:770375.

options.text: It increases the activity of epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in principal cells
options.explanation: Correct. More sodium is reabsorbed, and potassium and hydrogen ions are secreted.

options.text: It inserts aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct
options.explanation: No. That is ADH's action.

options.text: It blocks the sodium pump
options.explanation: No. Blocking the pump would reduce sodium reabsorption.

options.text: It reduces the filtration rate to zero
options.explanation: No. Its action is on the tubule.

explanation: Aldosterone acts on principal cells in the last part of the nephron, increasing ENaC activity. Sodium is reabsorbed; potassium and hydrogen ions are secreted in exchange.

text: The kidney keeps extra sodium. Why does the ECF grow instead of the sodium result rising?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Sterns RH. Disorders of plasma sodium — causes, consequences, and correction. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(1):55–65.

options.text: The kept sodium nudges osmolality up, ADH and thirst respond, and the extra water restores the concentration
options.explanation: Correct. Water follows sodium through the water system.

options.text: Sodium pulls water directly through the kidney without ADH
options.explanation: No. The water has to come from ADH and thirst.

options.text: Aldosterone also inserts water channels
options.explanation: No. Aldosterone acts on sodium channels.

options.text: The extra sodium moves into cells
options.explanation: No. Sodium is kept outside cells by the pump.

explanation: Keeping sodium raises osmolality slightly; the osmoreceptors switch on ADH and thirst; water is kept and drunk until the concentration returns. That's why the sodium system sets volume, not concentration.

text: Which of these does NOT directly trigger renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Tsilosani A, Gao C, Zhang W. Aldosterone-regulated sodium transport and blood pressure. Front Physiol. 2022;13:770375.

options.text: A fall in blood pressure reaching the kidney
options.explanation: No, this does trigger renin release.

options.text: Less sodium chloride reaching the macula densa
options.explanation: No, this does trigger renin release.

options.text: Sympathetic nerve activity
options.explanation: No, this does trigger renin release.

options.text: A rise in plasma osmolality
options.explanation: Correct. Osmolality drives ADH and thirst, not renin.

explanation: Renin release responds to renal perfusion pressure, sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa and sympathetic signals. Osmolality is the water system's signal.

text: A patient loses blood with no change in plasma osmolality. What happens to ADH?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Dunn FL, et al. The role of blood osmolality and volume in regulating vasopressin secretion in the rat. J Clin Invest. 1973;52(12):3212–9.

options.text: It stays off, because osmolality hasn't changed
options.explanation: No. Volume can switch ADH on by itself.

options.text: It rises, because a large fall in volume drives ADH regardless of osmolality
options.explanation: Correct. Volume takes priority over concentration.

options.text: It falls, to protect the sodium concentration
options.explanation: No. ADH rises.

options.text: It is replaced by aldosterone
options.explanation: No. Both systems respond.

explanation: A large fall in blood volume releases ADH non-osmotically and also lowers the osmotic switch-on point. When the systems conflict, the circulation is protected first.

text: A hyponatraemic patient had a diuretic dose an hour before the spot urine. Urine sodium is 45 mmol/L. How should you read it?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Spasovski G, et al. Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia. Eur J Endocrinol. 2014;170(3):G1–47.

options.text: It rules out low effective arterial blood volume
options.explanation: No. The diuretic may have raised the urine sodium.

options.text: It can't be used to exclude low effective arterial blood volume, because diuretics raise urine sodium
options.explanation: Correct. The cut-off only works without a recent diuretic.

options.text: It proves SIAD
options.explanation: No. A diuretic confounds that interpretation too.

options.text: It means the plasma isn't truly hypotonic
options.explanation: No. Urine sodium doesn't tell you that; measured plasma osmolality does.

explanation: The guideline's urine sodium cut-off of 30 mmol/L assumes no recent diuretic. A diuretic raises urine sodium and can send you down the wrong branch.

text: In patients with hypotonic polyuria, how did a copeptin-based approach after hypertonic saline compare with the classic water deprivation test?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Fenske W, et al. A copeptin-based approach in the diagnosis of diabetes insipidus. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(5):428–39.

options.text: It gave the right diagnosis more often (about 97% against 77%)
options.explanation: Correct. A copeptin above 4.9 pmol/L after hypertonic saline was more accurate.

options.text: It was less accurate but faster
options.explanation: No. It was more accurate.

options.text: The two were equally accurate
options.explanation: No. The copeptin approach performed better.

options.text: Copeptin can't be measured after hypertonic saline
options.explanation: No. That is how the test works.

explanation: In 144 patients, copeptin above 4.9 pmol/L after hypertonic saline gave the correct diagnosis in 96.5% of cases, against 76.6% for the water deprivation test.

text: Plasma osmolality 268 mmol/kg, urine osmolality 80 mmol/kg. What does this pattern suggest?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Spasovski G, et al. Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia. Eur J Endocrinol. 2014;170(3):G1–47.

options.text: ADH is appropriately off, and water intake is outrunning the kidney
options.explanation: Correct. Maximally dilute urine in dilute plasma means ADH is suppressed.

options.text: Non-osmotic ADH release from low arterial filling
options.explanation: No. ADH on would make the urine concentrated.

options.text: SIAD
options.explanation: No. In SIAD the urine is inappropriately concentrated.

options.text: Pseudohyponatraemia
options.explanation: No. The measured osmolality is low, so the plasma is truly dilute.

explanation: A urine osmolality of 100 mmol/kg or less with truly hypotonic plasma means ADH is off. The kidney is excreting free water but intake is outrunning it, as in primary polydipsia or very low solute intake.

text: Why don't the baroreceptors count the oedema fluid of a patient with heart failure?
author: Orville Malijan

references.title: Schrier RW. Body fluid volume regulation in health and disease: a unifying hypothesis. Ann Intern Med. 1990;113(2):155–9.
Schrier RW, Abraham WT. Hormones and hemodynamics in heart failure. N Engl J Med. 1999;341(8):577–85.
Levick JR, Michel CC. Microvascular fluid exchange and the revised Starling principle. Cardiovasc Res. 2010;87(2):198–210.

options.text: Oedema fluid has leaked out of the capillaries into the tissues, outside the circulation, so the arterial stretch sensors stay underfilled
options.explanation: Correct. The sensors respond to arterial filling, not total body fluid.

options.text: Baroreceptors only respond to osmolality
options.explanation: No. They are stretch sensors.

options.text: Oedema fluid has no sodium in it
options.explanation: No. It is extracellular fluid with sodium in it.

options.text: The kidney destroys the signal
options.explanation: No. The signal comes from the arteries.

explanation: The sodium system measures effective arterial blood volume through baroreceptors in the carotid sinus, aortic arch and left ventricle. Fluid pushed out of the capillaries into the tissues sits outside the circulation, so the arteries stay underfilled and the signals stay on.
